description: Remote sensing analyst and GIS developers
summary: EarthMeridian helps users whether an Earth measurement is really changing. The user chooses air temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind speed, or sunlight, then selects a country, province, district, or city. The app requests NASA POWER data for that area, keeps one value per year, and draws the time series beside a map. A straight-line fit and a Mann-Kendall test decide whether the trend is statistically significant. Both tests must have a p-value below 0.05. The same test can compare two places at the same level, shown on side-by-side maps. This matters because a hot place is not the same thing as a warming trend, and the same measurement can move in opposite directions in two regions. The result describes NASA’s grid cell for the selected area. It does not claim a cause.
details:
EarthMeridian answers the trend-detective challenge for any selected area, not only a fixed list of cities. The user picks one measurement and an area level: country, province, district, or city. Clicking a boundary sets the area. Run analysis loads the NASA POWER annual series for the grid cell at the center of that area, from 1981 through 2024, with at least 10 years. Rainfall is converted from a daily mean into a yearly total. The map colors temperature and sunlight by intensity, draws raindrops or humidity drops inside the area, and moves wind arrows in the wind’s direction. The chart shows the yearly series and the trend line. A second mode compares two areas of the same level on side-by-side maps.

The benefit is a clear verdict: the rate per year, the change over the full period, a 95% confidence interval, and two p-values. A significant result means both the straight-line test and the Mann-Kendall test are below 0.05. If they disagree, the signal is weak. The number is for NASA’s grid cell, not a street weather station, and it does not explain why the change happened.

The website is React and Vite. The API is Python and FastAPI. Statistics use pandas, NumPy, and SciPy, with the Mann-Kendall test written in the project. Maps use Leaflet, Natural Earth country outlines, and geoBoundaries for provinces and districts. Charts use Chart.js. The site is on Netlify and the API is on Render. NASA POWER, largely MERRA-2, is the measurement source.
